title: Amid the hunt for World Cup glory one of Tonga's greats is not done yet
text:
As Tonga's World Cup campaign prepares to hit fever pitch, Tui Lolohea cannot stop smiling even when the young bulls give him stick.

After a training session in the lead-up to Friday's match against Lebanon it is rising prop Demetric Vaimauga, who is the kind of guy you hear before you see, that gees Lolohea up.

"Awwww yeah, it's Mr I Ain't Done Yet!" Vaimauga crows as he grabs Lolohea by the shoulders.

That's what they called Lolohea in an Instagram post after he came off the bench for an injured Latu Fainu to set up a try in Tonga's 30-12 win over England last week and he's been copping it ever since.

It was a cameo Lolohea, at 31 and with Tonga enjoying more depth and talent in the halves than ever before, thought would never come.

But once it did it added to an already sterling legacy in the red jersey, tacking an extra chapter on a story that, against all odds, is still being written.

Lolohea has already played for Tonga more times than any other player in history and against the Cedars he'll extend his own record with his 23rd cap.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only player to have appeared in each of Tonga's five wins over Tier 1 nations, making them the only two constant faces in every image of Tonga's greatest days.

Loading Instagram content

Lolohea has been wearing these colours when those days were still just a dream. When he debuted for Tonga back in 2015, Fainu, the man he replaced last week and will partner in the halves on Friday, was only nine years old.

Vaimauga himself had just turned 11 and as the giant youngster runs away cackling, Lolohea fires back in Tongan through a grin and shakes his head.

"I knew I'd get stick for this. Mr I Ain't Done Yet — they're always taking the piss out of me," Lolohea said.

"I hope he gets banged next time he goes off the back fence, so I can go laugh at him.

"They joke around, but I am one of the oldest in the team and it's good to show you can run around with the young bucks."

Jason Taumalolo and Tui Lolohea have played in every one of Tonga's wins over Tier 1 nations. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yueng)

Lolohea and Taumalolo are the elders this time around as the two longest-serving players in the team by a mile and while Taumalolo dragged Tonga into a new world, Lolohea is very much a product of the old.

Watching his debut from 11 years ago against Samoa on the Gold Coast is a measure of how far things have come.

When the two meet again next week it will be in front of a sold-out crowd at Parramatta Stadium, which they probably could have filled twice over, and both sides will boast some of the best players in the world.

Back on Lolohea's first day, a little over 12,000 came through the gates and both nations had to choose between grey beards, who wanted to give back to their community, journeymen who knew this would be as good as it got, or youngsters before their big futures came for them.

International rugby league has come a long way since Tui Lolohea's Test debut. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Lolohea was one of the latter and at the time he was counted as one of rugby league's brightest prospects, with feet so fast tackling him was like trying to grab a handful of smoke.

So much has transformed since those times but according to Lolohea, the most important things have stayed the same.

"Why you're doing it, what you're representing, that never changes," Lolohea said.

"We're a little dot on the map and there's always talk about financial stuff but the pride of our island nation, the proud culture we put out to the people, we've built that over the years and the support from the people is massive.

Why Jason Taumalolo is still more than just a man for Tonga In the NRL, we only talk about what Jason Taumalolo can't do anymore. But when he pulls on the red of Tonga it's a reminder of what he still is and always will be for the island nation and for Test rugby league.

"That's what we want to represent, our people and our family names, where we come from.

"I was just a little kid back then. I remember the passion, for Tonga and Samoa, and we're on the big stage now but the passion is still there even though it was a long time ago."

Plenty of familiar faces from that night are still around. Kristian Woolf is still the coach, Sika Manu, Lolohea's first captain, is in camp as an assistant and Konrad Hurrell is the team's media manager.

But only Lolohea is still playing, making him the last son of the olden days before the heroes came back home.

He remembers frantically messaging Taumalolo in 2017, asking if he really was going to come back to Tonga and marvelling at what followed.

He cannot forget his intercept try in the win over New Zealand, head cocked back and laughing as he went over, or his late score in the semi-final against England that gave Tonga hope of a miracle, or of the trip back to the islands that followed, where the team was given medals of honour at the royal palace.

Amid a good NRL career for the Warriors and Wests Tigers before a lengthy stint in Super League, where he's spent the last eight seasons, including the last five with Huddersfield, Lolohea might never have fulfilled the club expectations he carried into his Tongan debut.

Instead, his finest hours have come for Tonga itself, for whom he is both pioneer and icon.

They've never won a big game without him and his reward has been honours that are usually bestowed on heroes of ancient wars.

His people have named trophies after him and he has been granted lands outside the family village of Lapaha by King Tupou VI.

The team's official nickname is Mate Ma' Tonga, which translates to "die for Tonga" but the memories Lolohea has helped create for his nation are immortal, like the win over Great Britain in 2019 or the breakthrough victory over Australia the following week.

Tui Lolohea has carved out a fine legacy in Tongan red. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

On the back of those glories a whole new generation of stars chose Tonga and players like Isaiya Katoa, Robert Toia, Leka Halasima and Tolu Koula have not just become part of the cause, they have taken it further.

They beat New Zealand again in the Pacific Championships two years ago and pushed Australia to the limit in the final. Lolohea, of course, played in both and set up a try in the latter.

Tonga are not here to compete anymore, they are here to win — against Australia, New Zealand, England, Samoa or anybody else who wants some.

Taking the World Cup itself back to Nuku'alofa is not an idle fantasy. It's a dream Tonga can hammer into reality as part of a new world order Lolohea and his generation helped create and somehow, he is still part of it.

Apart from Taumalolo, his only fellow survivor from 2017, the other legends from the old days are done.

Tui Lolohea has played in England for close to a decade now. (Getty Images via PA Images: Martin Rickett)

Between Katoa, Fainu and Junior Amone, Tonga have more class and options in the halves and the nation had every right to move on from Lolohea years ago.

But Lolohea himself is still here, refusing to be swept away, a lot older and a bit slower but as he showed against England, still capable of making a difference for the better.

"To still be here after all this time, I'm fortunate to be here again and running around with the young guys and some of the superstars of our game," Lolohea said.

"It's an honour, every time.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

"It's crazy to think, because I watch these guys every week and now I'm playing alongside them and I remember when we didn't really have any halfbacks at all.

"The depth we have now, it's such a big positive not just for now but for the years to come."

Lolohea knows this World Cup might be his last. He's finished up at Huddersfield and is still sorting out where he'll play next.

He is expected to drop back to the extended bench for next week's clash against Samoa and barring injury, it will be the same for the knockout stages.

This game against Lebanon could be it, the last time the legend of Tui Lolohea as a Tongan hero happens in front of us and not in our memories and that makes it worth savouring.

Tui Lolohea is hoping to build on his cameo appearance against England. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He played rugby league for Tonga more times than any other person who has ever lived but it is still a privilege to him, a prize beyond what he can ever say.

Even after all these years it still makes his father, Paul, smile and get as emotional as he ever does.

Growing up it was just the two of them. Lolohea's mother died when he was just one year old due a heart condition and if Friday is the end, father and son will be together for it.

But there might be a truth in the jokes the young fellas tell: Lolohea isn't done yet.

"He [Lolohea's father] flew in Tuesday morning, he'll be here for the next couple of weeks to enjoy the last ride, no matter what happens," Lolohea said.

"But we never know these days, do we? I'm just buzzing I got on the field again. I'm glad I got to play my part."

title: Cottesloe beaches shut as second dead whale washes ashore
text:
A second dead whale has washed up on a Perth beach, again prompting beach closures amid fears of increased shark activity in the area.

The 8-metre, significantly decomposed whale carcass washed up at South Cottesloe beach early today.

Cottesloe Mayor Melissa Harkins told 102.5 ABC Perth all the local beaches were closed while the council arranged for the whale's removal, including the Cottesloe main beach which has a shark barrier in place.

"I would encourage people if they're coming down to the Cottesloe area to stay out of the water for the time being until the carcass is removed and probably for a little while longer," Ms Harkins said.

She said council staff were planning to remove the carcass this morning.

"We are organising for dozers to come in because it's small enough that it would be able to fit on the back of a Town of Cottesloe truck and we'll remove it and it will go to landfill," she said.

The council have put in barriers and plan to remove the whale carcass today. (ABC News: Kate Leaver)

This is the second whale to wash up on a Perth beach in recent weeks.

On September 27 a 13-metre, 72-tonne humpback whale carcass washed up on south City Beach, which ultimately required a crane and cost almost $180,000 to remove.

title: Art students explore Rat Barbies, AI and two-sided human forms
text:
High school artists have been in the spotlight after 17-year-old student Jazz Lancaster Merton was crowned the 2026 Portrait Artist of the Year.

This month, secondary students in Western Australia's south-west region have had their chance to show their work in a professional setting, through a beloved community exhibition that has been running for 35 years.

Artist and arts educator Charlotte White, who was a judge at this year's Iluka Visions at Bunbury Regional Gallery, said it was an important launch pad for arts student careers.

Here are five artworks she says you should see at the exhibition:

I don’t think you see me — Emmasyn Dillon

Emmasyn Dillon's work won the Year 11 and 12 Best Overall Artwork at Iluka Visions. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

Emmasyn Dillon's mixed media sculpture received the Viewer's Choice Award and overall Best Year 11 and 12 Award.

White said she was captivated by the construction of the life-sized figure and the emotional depth to the two-sided sculpture.

"[It's amazing] to think about the technical skills to creating something like this, so not only thinking about a body sitting on a chair, but how that is going to be balanced with another figure coming out the back," she said.

"The more you look at this work, the more you can get out of it."

Rat Barbie — Remy Mathieson

The dolls and their costumes were constructed by Remy Mathieson. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

One of White's favourite works was Remy Mathieson's small doll-sized rat dolls, made with resin, paint, textiles, leather and wood.

"She's gone as far as to create custom costumes and they have little trinkets in their jackets, and there's character backgrounds next to each doll talking about who they are and what they do," she said.

"I almost want to see a story or a movie or something that like moves on from just these characters — I want to know more about them."

To Err is Human, To Forgive is Divine — Pia Mangano

Pia Mangano's work won the Year 11 and 12 3D Award. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

White said this work was selected for the best Year 11 and 12 3D Award because of its role as a thought-provoking and interactive conversational piece.

The question 'Does the inclusion of AI in art mean the end of human creativity?' is written under the sculpture and encourages viewers to ink their fingerprint under the 'yes' or 'no' column.

"It made me realise that these young artists are actually talking about big topics," White said.

"And it was really remarkable that they're not just creating art; they're inviting the audience to have a bit of a debate about things."

All That Floats Away — Beccy Mason

Beccy Mason's artwork titled All That Floats Away. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

The winner of the Year 9 and 10 Best Overall Artwork, All That Floats Away, was made out of cardboard, tissue paper, shellac, wire mesh and bamboo skewers.

White said it conveyed a sense of nostalgia and wonder.

"It had really a really interesting concept with a great use of those everyday materials and using them in a really interesting way," White said.

She also said the work was reminiscent of the renowned Japanese animation storytellers, Studio Ghibli.

"It had an imaginative, creative playfulness ... it's suspended and hanging within the gallery like it's sort of flying through."

It's a Wrap — Newton Moore Education Support Centre

Students from the centre collaborated on this bright and colourful work. (Supplied: Ashliegh Hodges)

White also highlighted this playful work of sticks wrapped in yarn, which was a collaboration between students at the Newton Moore Education Support Centre.

It's a Wrap won the Equity Award.

"I can imagine it was tricky for some to create this, but it's a really beautiful piece," White said.

"It's so colourful and textured; it's coming out from the wall and there's pom-poms and there's beads.

"We just really loved this work and how the students have created it together to create this really beautiful well-rounded piece."

Iluka Visions is at Bunbury Regional Gallery until November 15.

title: ABC reporter saves man from sinking car in floodwater north of Brisbane
text:
A driver has been rescued by two bystanders, including an ABC reporter, from his sinking car in floodwater north of Brisbane.

The man drove his four-wheel-drive at speed through water on Buchanan Road at Morayfield.

The car stalled and started to sink.

ABC reporter Will Murray swimming to the sinking car. (ABC News)

ABC reporter Will Murray and another man swam out to the car and pulled the driver out of the vehicle.

About 170 millimetres of rain has fallen in the area since this morning.

Speaking after a shower and some lunch, Murray said he was relieved everyone was OK.

"I saw him drive in and immediately his car started floating downstream so I rang Triple Zero," he said.

"On the phone the operator asked me if I could see the driver and if I thought he could get free.

"Initially I could see him, but he disappeared from my sight within seconds so I made the call to jump in."

Murray said he handed the phone to his colleague, camera operator Liz Pickering, and started swimming towards the sinking car.

The two rescuers pulled the man from the car just before it went under water. (ABC News)

"Another man quickly joined me and when we got to the car we tried to open the closest door, no luck, then got on the back of the car with the thought to break the back window," he said.

"I thought to try the passenger side rear door first and put my feet against the car and pulled as hard as I could and with some luck the door swung open.

"I think water rushing in helped create some pressure to force the door open."

Murray said the driver was then able to make his way to the open door, and the rescuers pulled him to safety and shallow waters.

"All three of us gave each other a big hug and were just so relieved," he said.

"It was very scary, but happy everyone is safe and relieved it is OK.

"I just witnessed how quickly it can go south and it is terrifying. Please don't drive into floodwaters."

The Queensland Fire Department advises all residents not to swim in floodwater.

'Saved that man's life'

Pickering was on scene filming overlay footage of the flooded road when the incident occurred.

She captured the incident on video as the men rescued the driver from the vehicle.

ABC reporter Will Murray and another man pull a man from a sinking car. (ABC News)

"The pair of them definitely saved that man's life," Pickering said.

"No doubt about that."

title: Former Australian sprint champion charged with child sex offence
text:
Australian sprint champion Jake Doran has been charged with a child sex offence.

The 26-year-old from Magnetic Island off Townsville was arrested last week after a police investigation into alleged indecent treatment of children between January 2025 and September 2026.

Mr Doran has been charged with one count of indecent treatment of a child under 16.

He was granted bail by police.

Australian Athletics ban

Australian Athletics said in a statement that based on information provided, it had imposed a provisional ban on Mr Doran, preventing him from attending club events or participating in athletics training.

"The former international athlete has no paid or unpaid role within Australian Athletics," a spokesperson said.

"The safety and wellbeing of all participants in our sport is paramount, and we take all allegations of this nature very seriously."

Jake Doran was arrested in Townsville. (Instagram)

Mr Doran is Australia's equal ninth fastest 100m sprinter with a personal best time of 10.15 seconds.

He made the semifinal at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022.

He previously won two national titles and represented Australia at two world championships.

Mr Doran's social media accounts and LinkedIn have recently been deactivated.

He is due to appear in the Townsville Magistrates court on November 5.

title: Potential PNG signing helping to heal Cooper Bai's family rift
text:
Marcus Bai has explained how he and son Cooper moved past the rift that fractured their family, as the Gold Coast forward edges closer to signing a deal with the PNG Chiefs.

Cooper was warmly greeted by his father at Port Moresby's Jacksons International airport yesterday after being granted permission to explore his options ahead of the opening of the November 1 contracting window.

The 19-year-old has been high on the Chiefs' list of targets since the club got the green light to enter the NRL in the 2028 season, with the forward proving a hit with local crowds in Papua New Guinea across his two-Test international career.

PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry The PNG Chiefs logo brings together elements representative of the country ahead of its NRL debut in 2028.

But Cooper's journey hasn't always been smooth, and last year he invoked the ire of his legendary Kumul father when he turned down a deal with Melbourne Storm to remain at the Titans.

"He promised one thing … and then he went and did the other thing, and I was cranky with him," Marcus told AAP.

"I said you've got to be fair and square, that's not how you treat the clubs and people.

"It's not good for us as a family, I was really pissed off with him for that, and I was really angry at him.

"Now [with the chance to join the Chiefs], I said go and have a look and you and your girlfriend sit down and [think through] before making a decision."

Cooper Bai angered his father Marcus (pictured) by going back on his word with regards to signing for the Storm. (Getty Images: Shannon Morris)

Marcus said Cooper had shown maturity by speaking to the Gold Coast to ask permission to visit the Chiefs.

Cooper was due to visit PNG on a family holiday after he was ruled out of the Kumuls' World Cup campaign with a hamstring injury.

"He's only young. He's still finding his feet, and if he comes here there will be a lot of pressure on him," Marcus said.

"The crowd here are tough, they tell you straight up [if they're not happy]."

The chance for Cooper to join the Chiefs would represent a full circle moment for the Bai family.

Marcus left Papua New Guinea in the 1990s to pursue a career as a professional rugby league player, going on to win titles in the NRL and Super League.

He would likely stand down from the Chiefs board if Cooper was to sign a deal to join the club for its inaugural season in 2028.

"I'm proud of his achievements, it is hard to do what he's done and to be able to have an interest from many clubs, it's pleasing for me as a father," Marcus Bai said.

AAP

title: NAB staff speak out after mass job cuts revealed
text:
National Australia Bank (NAB) workers have accused the banking giant of a "spill and fill" redundancy strategy, forcing entire teams to reapply for their positions as part of a sweeping restructure.

Earlier this week the major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June, including 1,500 before Christmas.

This is about 6 per cent of its total workforce, with corporate roles bearing the brunt.

Several workers who spoke to the ABC on condition of anonymity said the writing was on the wall as the bank pushed the uptake of AI and moved work offshore.

"Until today, it's been a lovely place to work," said Dylan*, who has worked in NAB's technology team for a decade but learnt he could be unemployed by the end of the year.

His team will have to reapply for their jobs in what is known as a "spill and fill" type of workforce restructure, where existing roles are made vacant and current employees have to fight for a smaller number of positions.

There is a two-week consultation period for Dylan's team and, for those being shown the door, their last day will be December 2 or 17.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au

Andrew Irvine says the changes are "expected to improve outcomes for customers". (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said in a note to staff he encouraged colleagues to be "thoughtful" and check in on one another, and indicated support would be offered to those "impacted personally".

The bank said in an ASX announcement that the mass redundancies, which are estimated to cost the bank about $300 million in restructuring costs, were part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers".

The bank declined to comment to the ABC on staff members' claims.

Jobs offshored

The looming redundancies have sparked serious concerns about offshoring among staff, as the banking heavyweight bolsters its Indian and Vietnamese headcount while it cuts staff based in Australia.

A leaked workforce plan seen by the ABC shows Dylan's team in technology, which consists of just under 500 people, is currently 53 per cent Australian-based.

The rest are based in NAB's offices in India (14 per cent), Vietnam (13 per cent), or are external contractors.

But, under the plan, the number of staff would be reduced to 400 by the 2027 financial year while the percentage of offshore workers would increase.

The Australian-based workforce would be cut to 40 per cent, with the Indian and Vietnamese offices upping their numbers to 30 and 20 per cent respectively.

NAB announced mass redundancies on Tuesday. (ABC News: Yiying Li)

James* resigned last Friday, just days before NAB announced it was going to slash staff, because of fears about the longevity of his business banking role.

He shared an email NAB sent in March, which stated the bank would be "expanding out teams in NAB India" to help in its goal of "focusing on digitising and simplifying processes, including increasing automation to speed up turnaround time" and "investing in our global teams".

James said the messaging in NAB had changed so drastically in the past six months that he no longer felt safe in his job and had left the banking industry.

"People are feeling the anxiety," he said, adding that he had moved to a service-based industry because, "I can't be replaced realistically for the next five to 10 years."

AI concerns

AI is also an issue on everyone's lips.

While there was no direct reference to AI, NAB did refer to "rapid technological change" in its announcement to the market and experts say its impact is clear.

MST Financial analyst Brian Johnson said that for a long time it was politically unacceptable to essentially replace people with AI.

Brian Johnson says it is becoming more acceptable to replace people with AI. (ABC News)

"We're probably approaching the point where it becomes more politically palatable to actually shed staff than perhaps it was even six months ago," he said.

"Technology will supplant a lot of functions at jobs. You can just do things better and faster."

Recruiter Clinton Marks from Robert Half said bank redundancies in 2026 appeared to be driven more by cost-cutting and organisational restructuring than direct AI replacement, despite growing pressure on executives to find productivity gains through technology.

Mr Marks said C-level managers were "under great pressure to reduce cost" and that "AI [is] an answer to those questions".

However, he said most organisations were not ready for large-scale AI deployment and he was not yet seeing workers replaced by the technology.

Instead, Mr Marks said, recent redundancy rounds were largely about reducing costs and streamlining operations, while demand remained strongest for workers with skills in cyber security, governance, risk, compliance and AI adoption.

'Wrecking ball'

The union representing bank employees said it was appalled by NAB's redundancy plans and dubbed it a "wrecking ball" to hit staff with the news so close to Christmas.

"Cutting 6 per cent of a workforce will not simplify NAB's operating model or better align its workforce to prioritise growth," Finance Sector Union (FSU) national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson said.

"It will wreak chaos and entrench a culture of anxiety at a bank that seems hell-bent on self-destruction.

"To take a wrecking ball to 6 per cent of one of Australia's largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB's leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers."

Nicole McPherson lambasted NAB's plans for its workforce. (Supplied)

Australian banks, large and small, have been cutting their workforces, with a major restructure at ANZ leading to thousands of job losses in the past year.

Last month, Bendigo and Adelaide Bank proposed cutting 137 jobs as part of an ongoing restructure.

The FSU has also said it had already seen 1,000 jobs cut so far this year at the Commonwealth Bank.

At the Commonwealth Bank's annual general meeting last week, the FSU asked if it could receive assurances workers' jobs were safe, prompting the bank to say there was "no ability to give a blanket commitment", adding that "AI is changing and complementing the way we work".

* Names have been changed to protect workers from potential negative repercussions.

title: Airbnb cracks down on check-out chores after travellers push back
text:
Airbnb guests will no longer have to strip beds, wash dishes or remove rubbish when checking out, under new rules to be introduced next month.

The changes have sparked anger among hosts, with some warning the crackdown could drive up costs and push smaller operators off the platform.

The short-term rental platform announced the changes on its website. They apply to reservations booked on or after November 20.

The changes come amid complaints from some travellers about being charged cleaning fees, which can cost hundreds of dollars, while also being expected to complete a list of chores before leaving a property.

The company said while cleaning fees would not be abolished completely, hosts could not require guests to perform tasks that took "significant time and effort or would normally be done by a cleaner".

Guests have complained that some of the tasks requested by hosts are onerous. (Unsplash: everdrop GmbH)

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb said in a statement.

"So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

Hosts can still ask guests to complete simpler tasks, such as placing used dishes in the sink and gathering used towels.

They will also continue to set their own cleaning fees.

Changes spark anger from hosts

Hundreds of hosts have criticised the new rules on Airbnb's online community forum.

Townsville Airbnb host Nadia Di Martino, who operates three listings from her Kirwin home, said the changes were "infuriating".

"I think that many hosts will either have to increase their prices and then pay someone else to do the whole cleaning," Ms Di Martino said.

She said she did the cleaning herself and did not charge guests a cleaning fee, but asked them to wash their dishes before checking out.

"I don't think it's unreasonable," she said.

She said she understood why Airbnb had acted, because some hosts had imposed excessive check-out chores.

But she said she was now considering leaving the platform and renting her rooms to students instead, or would ban the use of cooking facilities.

"I think that I would rather probably just … have permanent flatmates. I think it will be more comfortable for me," she said.

Nadia Di Martino shares her home with Airbnb guests. (www.airbnb.com.au)

Kendra, a host from South Carolina in the US, warned the policy could drive smaller hosts away from the platform and increase costs for guests.

"It's going to incentivise soulless, basic rentals and raise cleaning and liability costs that guests will ultimately bear the burden of," she said.

Mindy, from New Mexico, accused Airbnb management of being "so out of touch with the people cleaning vacation rentals", while Becky, from Canada, said she had "never been so upset by a policy change".

What does it mean for Australian travellers?

The changes apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform's global policy, including bookings in Australia.

Hosts will still be able to set house rules, including check-in and check-out times, limits on the number of guests, smoking restrictions, pet rules and quiet hours.

Airbnb said guests were still expected to leave properties in a reasonable condition and may be held responsible for damage or excessive cleaning caused by their stay.

title: Outback giant yabby Australia's latest 'big thing'
text:
Australia's "big things" are a common sight on a road trip, dotting highways and country towns, and a Queensland town has just added its own.

A giant yabby statue now stands in Windorah, 1,200 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

The big yabby was unveiled during a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Albert Street. (Supplied: Barcoo Shire Council)

It is a fitting addition to the town with a population of 100, best known for hosting "international yabby races", Barcoo Shire Mayor Sally O'Neil said.

"[At] Cooper Creek … you will pull up, go fishing, and you're bound to get a yabby or two, or five or more," she said.

Yabby races are a fixture on the annual Windorah social calendar. (ABC Western Qld: Heidi Sheehan)

It joins the collection of Australia's big crustaceans, including Ballina's big prawn and Cardwell's big crab, as well as other big things representing towns like Bowen's big mango, Tully's big gumboot and Woombye's big pineapple.

There are now several big crustaceans in Australia, like Ballina's Big Prawn.

Cr O'Neil said she hoped the $13,000 state-funded project would catch the eye of the town's next tourist.

"Hopefully it'll pull the tourists up and they may hang around an extra day … it's good for economic development of the communities out west," she said.

For Toowoomba artist — and now yabby sculptor — Jobella Bennett, the project reflects her journey into the artistic community, picking up the job after she began hosting classes in the central west.

"I got rung up and they [the council] were like, 'Could you make a yabby?'" she said.

"And I was like, 'Yeah, how big?'

"And they were like, 'As big as you can make it.'"

Jobella Bennett created the yabby with sheet metal and wire. (Supplied: Jobella Bennett)

Taking three months to build, measuring in at 4.6 metres and constructed from bird wire and sheet metal, the yabby is the largest artwork Ms Bennet has made.

"It's my first big project, I learned a lot," she said.

"I do a lot of research when I'm making anything that's new to me … so I did a bit of yabby research and just started making."

Ms Bennett said she hoped to work on more "big things", adding that it was important communities supported artistic creations.

"There's so many amazing artists out there and it's really nice that councils or the communities or whoever's organised it is actually backing artists," she said.

Crowds gather in Windorah to watch the yabby races. (ABC Western Qld: Heidi Sheehan)

Australia has professionalised 'big things'

University of the Sunshine Coast history lecturer Amy Clarke said while "big things" were also common in countries like Canada and the United States, Australia was bucking the trend in continuing to build more.

"Australia is still pedal to the floor, kind of, 'Let's build as many of them as we can,'" Dr Clarke said.

Jobella Bennett creates nature-inspired sculptures by hand. (Supplied: Jobella Bennett)

She said support for new statues across the country reflected their community involvement in comparison to the commercial incentive behind many American statues.

"And it is often the case that it is really a kind of group project," Dr Clarke said.

"It's often a chamber of commerce or the local council or a local charity group that's come together and said, 'How can we really celebrate and champion our town, and get people to come out here and visit us?'"

She said since the trend first began in the 1960s, it had become more official over time.

Australia's latest 'big thing' unveiled A group of mates have turned a pair of thongs into Australia's latest 'big thing', in the hopes of drawing tourists to their town.

"We've now seen over time a professionalisation of big things," she said.

"We now have a number of companies and professional fibreglass artists that specialise in making these sorts of giant objects.

"And you can tell as well when you look at them that they're intended to be quite artistic."

title: Meta fined $25b in US for deceiving users about Facebook privacy
text:
A judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $US25 billion ($35.6 billion) after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.

Facebook's deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J Mathew wrote in his ruling on Wednesday local time.

"Facebook promised users that they [the users] controlled their data. This was false," he said.

Raúl Torrez discusses the judgment during a news conference in Albuquerque. (AP: Susan Montoya Bryan)

Jurors in September found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users' personal data.

The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.

The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney-General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.

"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," he said.

Meta said the ruling and Mr Torrez's office's approach to enforcement "makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico".

"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal," CJ Mahoney, the company's chief legal officer, said in a statement.

Meta also reported on Wednesday better-than-expected quarterly revenue of $US64.6 billion ($92 billion), ahead of Wall Street estimates of $US63.37 billion ($90.32 billion).

New Mexico goes it alone

In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $US18 billion ($25.6 billion) and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.

The settlement ended a trial over teenage social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children's mental health.

The effort targeted features designed to grab young people's attention.

New Mexico did not join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.

Meta settles on harm to teens Meta has agreed to a settlement for court claims alleging its platforms harmed children.

During the trial, prosecutors cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed from Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg, in which he wrote that the company did not sell user data.

"You have control over how your information is shared," Mr Zuckerberg said.

"We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone."

Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $US35 billion ($49.8 billlion) to $US40 billion ($57 billion), arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price.

Meta's lawyers, meanwhile, argued that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation harmed New Mexicans.

They contended that the company should pay no more than $US3.4 billion ($4.8 billion), saying an award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up on appeal.

Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.

The $US25 billion ($35.6 billion) award far exceeds the $US5 billion ($7.1 billion) fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.

Villanova University associate law professor Peter Ormerod said he was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower.

"It comes out to about $US12,000 [$17,000] per person in New Mexico, and that's just a very large number. It's quite unlike anything else we've seen," Mr Ormerod said.

Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go toward state education spending.

But it could take years before the state sees any of the money while the company appeals.

Company argues that the state failed to prove harm

The state's case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from about 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica.

The now-defunct firm's clients included Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.

Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state's entire population, not just Facebook users, was deceived by the company.

They also said Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.

Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, says it plans to appeal. (Reuters: Carlos Barria)

Meta attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company's content moderation policies were robust and that freedom of speech must be considered.

They argued that the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements.

In one of the tech giant's few wins, jurors found that the state did not prove Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.

During a video deposition, Mr Zuckerberg denied the state's claims that Facebook profited off harmful content.

He said the company had to balance freedom of speech with content moderation.

Attorneys for the company said it had changed its policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it caught and removed an estimated 99 per cent of the content that violates its standards.

title: ‘It’s madness’: Safety fears prompt calls to bring back buttons on car dashboards

BusinessConsumer affairsRoad safety ‘It’s madness’: Safety fears prompt calls to bring back buttons on car dashboards Elias Visontay October 22, 2026 — 3:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Road safety advocates concerned that complex touch screen consoles in modern cars are distracting drivers and contributing to crashes want the government to consider forcing vehicle manufacturers to reintroduce physical buttons and dials for common and critical functions. The Australasian College of Road Safety’s (ACRS) call for the government to review whether existing safety standards have kept pace with increasingly complicated in-car controls comes at a turning point in the industry, including a push from insurance giant Allianz for automakers and authorities in all jurisdiction to take more seriously the distraction risk drivers face in modern vehicles. Experts have raised alarm at the trend away from physical buttons and controls towards touchscreen centre consoles with increasingly complex menus that distract drivers. Matthew Absalom-Wong Central to their concerns is that functions once performed by touch alone now require drivers to take their eyes off the road. While laws forbid drivers from holding mobile phones and severely restrict when they can touch a phone when legally mounted, rules governing integrated touchscreens are vague. Displaying video in motion is banned, but broader careless driving laws do not specify distractions linked to in-car controls. Testing from the Australian Automobile Association conducted by the University of Newcastle found the most poorly designed menus demand up to 11 taps to perform functions such as changing air conditioning or entering a navigation destination. This costs six seconds of visual attention, the study found. At a speed of 60 km/h, a driver travels about 100 metres blind in that time.

Advertisement

Earlier this year, China announced it will require physical buttons for critical controls in new cars sold in the country. While it doesn’t apply to the export market, it’s expected to shape vehicle design out of China when the law comes into effect from mid-2027. Related Article General insurance ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners As of this year, the Australasian New Car Assessment Program (ANCAP), which determines safety ratings for new cars in Australia, came into line with its European counterpart with new protocols that penalise an over-reliance on touchscreen menus. A manufacturer now loses points if it doesn’t provide either a physical button or stick or a permanently dedicated section of a touchscreen to engage indicators, hazard lights, windscreen wipers, headlights and sound the horn. However, a car penalised for distracting controls can recoup points in other areas to still achieve a 5-star overall rating. Ultimately, poor ANCAP ratings do not ban cars from the market. For Australia to follow in China’s path, the government would need to update the Australian Design Rules which govern the mandatory standards for all new vehicles in the market.

Advertisement

Dr Ingrid Johnston, chief executive of the ACRS, said there is now “a strong case for Australian authorities to review whether existing vehicle safety standards adequately address the distraction risks associated with modern touchscreen interfaces”. She said existing rules do not comprehensively assess the distraction or complexity associated with operating in-vehicle systems. Johnston said that when updating the requirements, authorities should consider the number of interactions required to complete common tasks, the time drivers spend looking away from the road, and whether complex functions should be restricted while driving. Related Article Road safety Chinese ban on Tesla-style door handles likely to flow through to Australia “ACRS would support consideration of stronger, evidence-based requirements, including whether frequently used or safety-critical functions should have physical controls or other interfaces that remain readily accessible without requiring prolonged visual attention,” Johnston said. Allianz, in calling for stricter car design rules, pointed to the findings of research it commissioned comprising a review of 80 studies on driver distraction, as well as new experiments using retina-tracking technology in real vehicles and analysis of claims data and more than 34,000 injury-causing crashes since 1999.

Advertisement

The review reassessed historical crashes for additional indicators of distraction such as a lack of braking or evasive action. While distraction is recorded as the cause in just 1.4 per cent of crashes, Allianz now believes distraction contributes to as many as one in three road crashes. Allianz also released survey data of Australian motorists which found 75 per cent of the 1200 respondents believe in-vehicle technology distractions have increased in recent years, with 41 per cent rating the risk of driver distraction as high or very high. About 29 per cent of respondents said they experienced a critical situation, such as hard braking, a near miss or a crash, while using a vehicle touchscreen. One in five Australian drivers surveyed reported causing or partly causing a crash in the past three years, with 67 per cent of those saying distraction definitely or possibly played a role. “Allianz’s studies also assessed how a distracted driver’s performance compared with an intoxicated driver, and found in certain scenarios such as on rural roads, a two-second glance away from the road can be more dangerous than a 0.08 blood alcohol content in a driver,” the review said. Michael Regan, an emeritus professor at the University of NSW who has studied road user behaviour and in-vehicle distraction, was critical of newer generation cars that required a touchscreen to adjust settings such as side mirrors, air conditioning and radio.

Advertisement

“It’s madness because it’s extremely distracting,” Michael Regan, emeritus professor at UNSW “It’s madness because it’s extremely distracting,” said Regan, who oversaw Allianz’s findings. “We know from research that when a driver takes their eyes off the road, they typically miss traffic signs, signals and subtle changes, and that means they take longer to react in the presence of danger, largely because they haven’t been able to predict it.” Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Uber forced to reinstate driver accused of speeding, sexual comments Regan cited studies which have found that when a driver looks away from the road for more than two seconds, their risk of having a crash doubles, and for every second after that the “risk rises exponentially”. “You’re not only taking you’re eyes off the road, you’re taking your mind off the road,” Regan said.

Advertisement

Whether car manufacturers agree to stricter design rules is unclear. Tony Weber, chief executive of the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries, which represents the industry, said Australia acting ahead of other jurisdictions could harm local supply and cost. “International harmonisation ensures Australians benefit from globally developed vehicle safety standards. Introducing additional Australian requirements could increase complexity and cost for consumers,” Weber said. A spokeswoman for Transport Minister Catherine King also noted the importance of international harmonisation for Australian Design Rules due to the nation’s reliance on vehicle imports. “The Australian government is continually adding to or amending Australian Design Rules (ADRs) based on changing vehicle technology and road safety risks,” she said. Amplia Therapeutics has delivered a sweeping update on its four-front clinical assault with lead drug narmafotinib, targeting some of the toughest cancers, including pancreatic, ovarian and lung cancer. Headlining the progress snapshot is an intriguing new clue from its key pancreatic cancer trial, suggesting the drug’s effectiveness may not depend on whether a patient’s tumour carries certain cancer-driving mutations in the KRAS gene. KRAS gene mutations are genetic changes that can cause cells to grow and divide uncontrollably, helping drive disease development. The gene normally acts like an on-off switch, controlling signals that tell cells when to grow. When mutated, the switch can become permanently stuck in the “on” position, encouraging cancer cells to multiply. Amplia Therapeutics is pushing ahead with four clinical trials for its lead drug narmafotinib in pancreatic, ovarian, and lung cancer (pancreatic cancer cells pictured). The finding is significant as pancreatic cancer treatment is rapidly shifting towards targeted therapies. KRAS gene mutations are found in more than 90 per cent of pancreatic cancers, making them a major focus for drug developers. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently approved a new KRAS-targeting drug that showed a significant survival benefit, highlighting the potential of this new class of therapies. Amplia’s data, however, suggest its Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) inhibitor narmafotinib could work alongside the KRAS drugs, potentially making it effective in a broader patient population or in powerful combination treatments.

Advertisement

‘It is exciting to be moving forward with these trials as the company build on positive clinical data.’ Amplia Therapeutics chief medical officer Dr Jason Lickliter Narmafotinib works by blocking a protein known as FAK, which is found at unusually high levels in solid tumours such as pancreatic cancer. The protein plays a key role in helping cancer cells grow, survive and resist treatment. FAK also contributes to the creation of dense, scar-like fibrotic tissue that forms a protective fortress around some tumours. By blocking FAK, the company believes narmafotinib can weaken or even break down this biological barrier, giving chemotherapy a cleaner shot at destroying the cancer cells within. Amplia’s ACCENT trial, which is evaluating narmafotinib combined with standard chemotherapy in newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic cancer patients, has delivered promising results. Previously reported data showed a significant response rate of 36 per cent, a median overall survival of 11.1 months and a complete response rate of a stunning 7.8 per cent, a figure considered historically rare in pancreatic cancer. The latest findings suggest the treatment may also have serious staying power, with two patients now having clocked a remarkable two years in the study and a third still receiving treatment after 19 months. Amplia Therapeutics chief medical officer Dr Jason Lickliter said: “It is exciting to be moving forward with these trials as the company builds on the positive clinical data from the ACCENT trial and the promising preclinical data underpinning the PRROSE and Lilly combination studies.”

Advertisement

While its ACCENT trial continues to deliver, the company has also advanced three other clinical trials into the late-stage start-up phase. The first, dubbed ACCENT-Mini, is being designed to evaluate a daily dosing regimen of narmafotinib in addition to chemotherapy at three Australian sites. Ethics approval is expected imminently, with safety and pharmacokinetic data anticipated in the first half of 2027. Management says this data will be crucial for its submission to the US FDA for a larger registrational study. The company is also tackling ovarian cancer with its PRROSE study, opening a second major front for its lead drug. The Australia New Zealand Gynaecological Oncology Group will run the trial in collaboration, sponsoring and coordinating it through its extensive network of more than 1650 members. Like ACCENT-Mini, the PRROSE trial will pair narmafotinib with established chemotherapy drugs, this time carboplatin and paclitaxel, targeting women with high-grade serous ovarian cancer who have shown a limited response to their initial treatment. The main goals are to assess the combination’s safety and explore whether it can increase the proportion of patients eligible for successful surgical resection. With the trial protocol finalised and ethics approval submitted, Amplia is nearing recruitment of 26 patients across Australia and New Zealand.

Advertisement

Rounding out the pipeline, the company is preparing a separate update on its trial combining narmafotinib with global pharmaceutical giant Lilly’s experimental KRAS G12C inhibitor, olomorasib. The study will target patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer, exploring the potential of attacking the disease on multiple fronts by combining drugs that target different cancer-driving pathways. Amplia believes blocking the FAK protein could help shut down a pathway cancer cells use to resist KRAS-targeted treatments. With four trials pushing ahead across a range of hard-to-treat cancers, Amplia appears to be methodically building a case for its cancer drug narmafotinib. The suggestion that its lead drug could work independently of the KRAS mutations that dominate pancreatic cancer might just be the key to unlocking its potential as a standalone or combination therapy in a field crying out for new options. Senior public servants repeatedly queried why NSW One Nation leader Mike Newman was charging taxpayers for hotels, trips and restaurant bills, including a $7791 dinner with a Japanese trade delegation which included 71 beers and 23 bottles of wine. Documents released through parliament on Thursday show senior bureaucrats rebuked Newman for his spending habits during his 28-month stint as a senior trade commissioner in Japan, with one executive rejecting a $211 bill for lunch and telling the now-One Nation leader it was “not how the NSW government does business”. It comes after this masthead last week revealed Newman racked up hundreds of thousands of dollars in expenses for taxpayer-funded flights, five-star hotels and restaurant and bar bills during his 28-month stint as a senior trade commissioner in Japan. The spending included about $20,494 on a seven-month stay in a Meriton Suite in Sydney before he moved to Japan. The spending occurred while he waited for permission to travel to Japan during the COVID-19 pandemic, despite Newman living in Sydney when he was appointed.

Advertisement

He was also charging taxpayers about $8000 a month to rent an apartment in Tokyo for some of that time. The spending was revealed in the context of Newman’s repeated criticisms of the NSW public service since his appointment as One Nation’s leader in NSW, in which he raised the prospect of “claw[ing] back entitlements from those found responsible for having egregiously misused public funds without consequences”. Mike Newman is the candidate for Cessnock and the One Nation leader in NSW. James Brickwood “There is so much money and waste that is inside the public service,” he said during his unveiling in August. But the documents released on Thursday shed new light on some of the expenses, as well as revealing the public service repeatedly questioned Newman’s spending. This masthead previously reported Newman charged taxpayers for a bill adding up to almost $5300 at Crystalbrook Kingsley, a hotel in Newcastle, in August 2023. He said that had been for a dinner with a Japanese trade delegation and spending on alcohol was pre-approved.

Advertisement

But the documents show the bill was larger – $7790.50 – and reveal public servants said they were only told that alcohol would be served at the event. The bill, for 51 people, included a three-course meal at $109 per head, as well as 71 beers and 23 bottles of wine. The restaurant charged $59 per bottle. The documents show that spending was later closely scrutinised, with an official forced to answer a series of questions about how it had occurred. The official – whose name was redacted – noted that only one onshore Investment NSW staffer was at the event, and that Newman had “hosted the dinner”. The dinner was aimed at “facilitating connections” with the Japanese delegation, NSW officials and “academia” and “fostering ongoing dialogue”, they wrote, and resulted in “further discussions” on potential “partnerships and investment opportunities”. The official said they had found out Newman and the Department of Regional NSW had been planning “some kind of dinner” about a month earlier. However, they said, it was “only at the event itself that we found out that alcohol was being served and that Mike Newman was intending to pay for all of it”.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes The long list of former Coalition MPs seeking new home on One Nation’s crowded NSW ticket Newman previously defended his spending and pointed to cases of using his own money to fund trips, such as in October 2023, when he said he spent about $10,000 to attend an Australia-Japan Business Council event in Melbourne because the government would not approve it. Some documents also show Newman paid his own per diem during some business trips. The One Nation leader said he had saved taxpayers by arguing against a $49 million net zero economy office the government wanted to establish, though this masthead has been unable to verify that claim. “I should be bloody given congratulations, not censured, for stopping a $50 million empire going in that was going to be a complete waste of money,” he said. Not all the documents obtained through a parliamentary call for papers have been publicly released, and Newman said there was important “contextual” information in emails he had sent to the department.

Advertisement

“Senior management and I did not see eye to eye because we had very strong differences of opinion on doing business,” he said. “My department wanted to issue a fatwa on me [and] they used to use technicalities and irrelevant stuff to go after me because I threatened the status quo. “I’m not a hypocrite, I was paying for a lot of this stuff myself.” Among the other expenses was another month-long stay at the Meriton Suites in North Sydney in 2023 for which he billed taxpayers $5086. Documents show public servants questioned that spending, and wrote to Newman asking why he was staying in the hotel for 32 nights, longer than had been approved. The public servant notes the department had approved 25 days despite already having “concerns [it] was an extensive period out of market”. “What’s the reason for the extra first week before the approved travel date?” they wrote.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

One Nation Revealed: One Nation leader’s seven-month Sydney hotel stay that cost taxpayers $20,000 Newman – who also took personal leave during that period – said he had booked a longer trip to get a discount, and had paid for his own personal leave as well as his accommodation while in Newcastle for the Crystalbrook Kingsley event. It is unclear if all of the spending revealed through the documents was approved. However, in another, a public servant noted they would reject a $211 bill Newman had sought to charge taxpayers for a business lunch at Glorietta in North Sydney. “At $70 per head (including wine), this exceeds a reasonable cost for lunch, noting that such hospitality and entertainment is not how the NSW government does business with the private sector,” the official wrote. Newman said the meal had been with a senior executive, and that the client had ordered a $17 glass of wine and another Investment NSW staff member had ordered an expensive prawn salad. “I could hardly take a person like that to the food hall at North Sydney station,” he said. title: Ping-pong tables won’t save your office – but these 10 things will
text:

BusinessWorkplaceJobs Opinion Ping-pong tables won’t save your office – but these 10 things will Tim Duggan Work columnist October 22, 2026 — 2:30pm

October 22, 2026 — 2:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Many years ago, we had a ping-pong table in our office. At the time we thought it was the coolest perk in the world – a way for employees to play and let off steam most afternoons. It now feels like a quaint inclusion, especially when modern workplaces spend big dollars on ways to engage their staff, from overseas meet-ups to long lunches, on-site wellness centres to ergonomic workstations. Once the ultimate indicator of office perks, the table tennis table now is less common in modern workspaces. Bloomberg However, none of that matters if you don’t have a healthy work environment in the first place. Instead of throwing money at the problem, here are 10 small, repeatable behaviours that anyone can do to improve their workplace right now, without waiting for the ping pong table to arrive. 1. Swap meetings for walks. The next time you have a one-on-one meeting with a colleague that doesn’t require a screen, suggest that you take it outside. Walk around the block, or to the closest park, and you’ll have better conversations and get more exercise than spending yet another meeting staring at the blank office wall.

Advertisement

2. Give credit where it’s due. The simplest way of showing appreciation is by acknowledging it in public. When someone does something that’s worth praising, say it out loud, on the spot, ideally to their face. Extra points if you also voice it in an all-staff meeting, or on a group email, so everyone can see. 3. Ask more questions than you answer. The smartest person in the room is the most curious. When you ask questions with an open mind, you’re ensuring you properly understand what’s going on. You never want to be the person who just talks over everyone, so listen more than you speak. Any one of these can save you money, time, pain and heartache if you incorporate them into your everyday working life. 4. Treat mistakes as learning opportunities. Everyone stuffs up, but it’s what you do next that sets the cultural tone. When you weaponise mistakes so that people are too scared to fail, you’re creating a toxic work environment. Think of every error as a way of improving the process so that it’s even better the next time. 5. Set expectations and meet them. The simplest definition of trust is what happens when you set clear expectations and meet them. In the workplace, tell your colleagues what you’re going to do, and then do it. That builds trust over the long term, one of the key components of a healthy working environment.

Advertisement

6. When in doubt, over-communicate. Work is a team sport, and you should include as many people as possible in the successes that you can. One way to do that is to over-communicate – not by CCing the world on every email, but by bringing people along so they understand the why behind your actions. Editor's pick Opinion

Holidays Why it’s time for you to ditch taking long annual holidays Tim Duggan Work columnist 7. Treat leave as leave. When someone’s out of the office, let them be out of the office. It doesn’t matter whether it’s sickness, bereavement, maternity or annual leave, give people the mental space to not think about work when they’re not there. 8. End every meeting with an action. We’ve all been in meetings that last forever and then end with nothing much to show for it. Close out every single meeting with at least one action item, then write it down to ensure it’s followed up on. 9. Make generous assumptions. Of course, you can be wary of other people’s motivations, but what might happen if you made “generous assumptions” instead? These are the beliefs that someone is acting with good intentions instead of automatically assuming they are not. It can really change how you think about everyone around you.

Advertisement

10. Give good handovers. The difference between success and failure in a project is often the quality of the handover. This means fully explaining the progress of where things are at – both good and bad – every time you move roles, go on leave, or finish up at a job. Any one of these can save you money, time, pain and heartache if you incorporate them into your everyday working life. Recognition, feedback and productive workplaces are linked with higher engagement, retention, and healthier teams. These simple habits don’t cost a cent, but they are really worth their weight in gold. title: Haines' staff speak of 'deeply traumatic' experience caring for MP in aftermath of attack
text:
In brief Supporters are rallying around the MP as the wait for further updates on her condition continues.

The man accused of attacking Helen Haines will remain behind bars.

The office of Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition, has said its members are "devastated" by the attack on the independent MP, adding that their proximity to the incident had made the experience "deeply traumatic".

"Our team is devastated by the attack on Helen Haines this week. Helen is adored by her team. She is a remarkable leader, a truly wonderful boss and someone we all care about deeply," Kaz Rourke, Helen Haines' chief of staff, said in a statement released on Thursday afternoon.

"Most of us were in the office when the incident occurred, and some of us were involved in Helen's immediate care, so this has been deeply traumatic for the team," she added.

"We are receiving a great deal of support and my priority right now is making sure Helen's staff are as okay as they can be. I'm so very proud of them and know Helen would be too."

She added that, while Haines' office remained closed to the public, the team was "working in the background and planning towards reopening later next week".

"It is important to us to keep doing our jobs, for Helen and for the people of Indi.

"Most of all, our hearts right now are with Helen, with Phil, their children and their family."

'Helen is alive and she's stable'

Melbourne's Alfred Hospital has said Haines remains in a critical condition and her husband Phil confirmed on Wednesday that the MP has had both her legs amputated and is recovering from multiple surgeries.

"But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable," he told reporters inside the hospital.

"That is the most important thing for our family."

Governor-General Sam Mostyn said she had the "great honour" to spend time with their broader family before the press conference.

"She's lost both her legs in this horrific attack and how any person, let alone a family then starts to process that," Mostyn told ABC News Breakfast.

"We've just got to continue to have them in our thoughts."

Supporters gathered in Wodonga for a vigil for Indi MP Helen Haines. Source: SBS News / Rayane Tamer

Independent MP Dai Le told SBS Vietnamese she had a "wonderful" conversation with Haines in the most recent parliamentary sitting week.

"Helen told me she was looking forward to the end of the year so she could have some rest. That last conversation with her has stayed with me."

The member for Fowler said it's "very difficult and confronting" to hear what has happened to Haines.

"My thoughts are with her, her husband and their family. It’s also an incredibly difficult time for the Nugent family [Brendan Nugent is accused of the attack], who know Helen. It’s hard to comprehend what has happened, and I feel for everyone involved."

Le said she was determined to keep up her community engagements.

"I will not stop attending community events or surround myself with security simply because of what has happened. I’m part of the people."

A sea of orange cockatoos

The update has brought some relief to her supporters across the electorate, including her predecessor Cathy McGowan.

McGowan won the seat of Indi in 2013, serving as the electorate’s first-ever independent MP until she retired in 2019.

She said the shock is still moving through the community.

Supporters filling a book with well wishes for Helen Haines at a vigil in Wodonga. Source: SBS News / Rayane Tamer

"If it can happen to Helen, it can happen to anybody," she told SBS.

"We no longer think, in rural and regional Australia, with our strong communities, that we're immune.

"It was one of us, in our community, by one of us, and saved by us as well."

Supporters in Wodonga gathered for a vigil on Wednesday evening. Many had brought a cardboard orange cockatoo with them — a symbol throughout Haines' campaign.

Among them was Wodonga resident Susan Gordon-Brown. After moving to the area around a year and a half ago, she says she "can't think of anyone better to help".

"She has this huge constituency, yet she seems to be everywhere," she said.

Wolfgang Huber has been involved in every election Haines and McGowan have been in.

He said both have been really important for the community.

Wolfgang Huber holding his prized orange cockatoo. Source: SBS News / Rayane Tamer

"We are a community that has come from all over the world and we should treasure that," he said.

"If I zip it, I look like any other Australian.

"But as soon as I open my mouth, they'll say 'oh, you're a migrant', and that hurts."

What's next for her alleged attacker?

The man accused of attacking Haines will remain in custody until early next year, while an investigation into the incident continues.

Brendan Nugent has been charged with dangerous driving, intentionally causing serious injury, and a federal offence of causing harm to a public official. Court documents showed additional charges for cultivating and possessing cannabis.

Brendan Nugent faced Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. Source: AAP / Anita Lester

He did not apply for bail and was taken to Melbourne Assessment Prison.

The 43-year-old's next court appearance is scheduled for 4 February 2027, for a committal hearing.

It's alleged he intentionally struck the 65-year-old MP with his Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northern Victoria, on Monday afternoon.

title: 'Imagine siding with the tech bros': Pocock proposes new levy on big players
text:
In Brief David Pocock has proposed a 5 per cent levy on data centres to generate $500 million by 2030.

Speaking at the National Press Club, the senator suggested independents form a coalition for minority government.

Independent senator David Pocock has called for a levy on data centres he says would raise $500 million by the end of the decade.

He said the government was "starstruck" by foreign AI companies and blind to public sentiment, failing to respond to concerns over the impacts of data centres on communities.

Speaking at the National Press Club, he outlined his vision for a political system beyond the major parties, and suggested independents could form a coalition to govern in minority.

The ACT senator suggested smaller community-interest parties working alongside independents could deliver evidence-based solutions, and shift the national focus to the long term.

Pocock also praised his friend Helen Haines, describing her as "a beacon of integrity".

Haines remains in a critical condition after she was allegedly attacked by a 4WD driver outside her parliamentary office in Wangaratta on Monday.

Data centres

Pocock proposed introducing a 5 per cent levy on data centres from early next year. He said the idea had been costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office and would generate $500 million by 2030.

It would be enough, he said, to cover a year of spending for the Housing Australia Future Fund, contributing to the development of new social and affordable housing.

"We all pay income tax to fund the services we use and rely on, yet these huge multinationals turn over billions and find ways to pay little to no company tax here," he said.

Pointing to a lack of long-term thinking, he said the government is putting data centres and frontier AI development ahead of communities and creatives.

"Imagine siding with the tech bros over almost every Australian author, artist and journo that wants their copyright protected," he said.

Pocock, a member of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, cited evidence from the Copyright Agency's CEO, who warned Australia risked becoming "a global data laundering hotspot" without stronger copyright protections.

A meeting of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in October. Source: AAP / Sarah Wilson

Independents working together

Pocock said the current major party system is "letting us down" by prioritising vested interests over community needs.

"Too often people are telling politicians how tough things are, only to get some talking points or a long government shopping list of things they’ve done in response," he said.

"And so people are turning away, turning towards something different or turning off altogether."

Rather than "recycled political candidates, former staffers and others from the political class", he wants more independents to choose to represent their communities, while also contributing to a broader political collective on issues like accountability, gambling and the environment.

The ACT senator said smaller community-focused parties and independents working together would better reflect Australia's regional and generational diversity than the traditional two-party system.

"Australians want a politics where their local representative actually reflects their community’s view — not the position of a party or other vested interest," he said.

He said his model prioritised community needs, the opinions of experts and solutions-oriented thinking.

"We want people who have courage and a commitment to the long-term solutions needed to solve them. People like Dr Helen Haines," he said.

Pocock described Haines as "the MP we all wish we had", emphasising her dedication to democracy, transparency, accountability, care and kindness.

title: Elon Musk has hinted at a SpaceX-Tesla mega merger. Could it really happen?
text:
In brief Special committees have been set up to discuss a union between SpaceX and Tesla.

The possible merger news has sent shares of SpaceX surging.

Elon Musk said he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public on Wednesday (AEDT), driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.

Asked on a call with analysts about a possible merger, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield", but that a combination would be "a good idea".

Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly 5 per cent in after-hours trading following the comments.

Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders.

He added that he could not take part in the talks because of a conflict of interest.
