The committees have not agreed on any deal terms, and Musk said there is no guarantee they will, cautioning that treating a merger as certain would be overstating it.

Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle".

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

Musk has in the past tantalised shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays bank suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.

What could a SpaceX-Tesla merger look like?

While Tesla and SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, satellite communications, and computing infrastructure, including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit.

A merger would create a single integrated company at the centre of Musk's long-term vision.

"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab [a planned huge semiconductor fabrication plant] obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation [data centres in space], connectivity," Musk said on Wednesday.

Bringing the companies together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Musk's projects already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity.

Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence.

What does it mean for investors?

Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses.

A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about US$3.5 trillion ($4.98 trillion).

Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent.

Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another.

Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together?

Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future data-centre projects.

Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Musk hopes it can start volume production by late 2028.

Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship rocket production, while SpaceX technologies have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster vehicle.

A merged company could also coordinate efforts to secure strategic supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite hardware.

What are the risks?

The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation.

SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and NASA. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing.

READ MORE Ukraine depends on this battlefield advantage. Others call the shots

The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow.

Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and space infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

Mostyn: 'Australians are yearning for kindness'

Governor-General Sam Mostyn said the country must come together and support each other.

"What does a nation do now?" she asked.

"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack, reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened, who are still trying to cope with this."

"We need to offer everyone comfort to get through this, to celebrate our strong and stable system of government and parliaments and democracy, and be proud of that."

She encouraged Australians to remind themselves, as Helen said all the time, that they "have good hearts".

"Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they're asking us why we lost the great skill of disagreeing well and with decency to each other," she said.

She said not everyone had to agree, but she encouraged people to "wrestle the issue", not the person.

"It's important to remember, words matter, whether spoken or in written form, or increasingly in the virtual world," she said.

"In the midst of what is a disturbing and distressing moment, particularly for Helen's family and her friends and her team, everyone who loves her, let's work together as a healing force."

title: Pregnancy discrimination remains widespread in Australian workplaces
text:
IN BRIEF Nearly half of mothers report discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or returning to work.

An Australian Human Rights Commission report found pregnancy discrimination hasn't decreased over the last decade.

After being passed up for an associate principal role at a school, a woman went on maternity leave to have her first baby.

When she returned to work, she expected to go back to her role in leadership.

Instead, her principal told her she would come back as a music teacher.

"He just said, the school no longer needed my role," the Perth woman told AAP.

"I don't have any formal music qualifications ... He gave me the job he considered to be the least important."

The mother-of-two, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as she still works in the state school system, considered taking action against her principal.

She spoke to the Fair Work Ombudsman and her union, but decided not to pursue a claim.

"My life was already so full, I didn't want to take more time away from being with my kid," she said.

"And it would just be rough to work for someone that you had legally fought with to have that job."

READ MORE Gabriela was playing at the top of her sport. Then she fell pregnant

In another case, Alana, from Melbourne, worked at a hydrotherapy service for babies and tried to take time off to be with her one-year-old when he was hospitalised.

"I gave a few days' notice, and she [the manager] got really, really angry and lost it, and said it's unacceptable, if your son is sick, you have to call your mother or a babysitter," she said.

"Another time he was sick ... she said that I had to have my husband take him, or I wouldn't have a job."

Almost half of mothers, 49 per cent, experienced discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or return to work, a 2014 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) study found.

Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody says pregnancy discrimination and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility remains widespread. Source: Getty / Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images

About 91 per cent did not lodge formal complaints out of stress, fear of retaliation or lack of legal awareness.

Little has changed, with pregnancy, breastfeeding and family responsibility discrimination remaining "a significant and widespread workplace issue" in 2026, an AHRC report released on Tuesday found.

The number of alleged pregnancy discrimination complaints the AHRC received rose from 54 in 2021 to 72 in 2025.

The AHRC met with 84 stakeholders, including industry, community, advocates, lawyers, unions and academics.

READ MORE Pregnant women face widespread workplace discrimination, report finds

Recurring patterns of discrimination were identified, including "sham" redundancies and job loss during pregnancy or parental leave, diminished duties when returning to work, and refusal of flexible work arrangements.

Harms were amplified for First Nations, migrant, racially-marginalised, disabled, and LGBTQI+ communities, who experienced intersecting forms of discrimination.

"It was really clear that pregnancy discrimination, and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility, is widespread and hasn't changed significantly in the last 12 years," Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody said.

She said employers needed to change how they conceptualise work, with flexible working arrangements made a presumption unless an employer rebuts, and the 12-month service requirement to access unpaid parental leave eliminated.

The AHRC made 18 recommendations, including amending the Sex Discrimination Act to ban indirect discrimination based on family responsibilities, and limiting redundancies during or immediately after parental leave.

Road safety advocates concerned that complex touch screen consoles in modern cars are distracting drivers and contributing to crashes want the government to consider forcing vehicle manufacturers to reintroduce physical buttons and dials for common and critical functions. The Australasian College of Road Safety’s (ACRS) call for the government to review whether existing safety standards have kept pace with increasingly complicated in-car controls comes at a turning point in the industry, including a push from insurance giant Allianz for automakers and authorities in all jurisdiction to take more seriously the distraction risk drivers face in modern vehicles. Experts have raised alarm at the trend away from physical buttons and controls towards touchscreen centre consoles with increasingly complex menus that distract drivers. Matthew Absalom-Wong Central to their concerns is that functions once performed by touch alone now require drivers to take their eyes off the road. While laws forbid drivers from holding mobile phones and severely restrict when they can touch a phone when legally mounted, rules governing integrated touchscreens are vague. Displaying video in motion is banned, but broader careless driving laws do not specify distractions linked to in-car controls. Testing from the Australian Automobile Association conducted by the University of Newcastle found the most poorly designed menus demand up to 11 taps to perform functions such as changing air conditioning or entering a navigation destination. This costs six seconds of visual attention, the study found. At a speed of 60 km/h, a driver travels about 100 metres blind in that time.

Advertisement

Earlier this year, China announced it will require physical buttons for critical controls in new cars sold in the country. While it doesn’t apply to the export market, it’s expected to shape vehicle design out of China when the law comes into effect from mid-2027. Related Article General insurance ‘Humans make mistakes’: Insurer offers discount to self-driving car owners As of this year, the Australasian New Car Assessment Program (ANCAP), which determines safety ratings for new cars in Australia, came into line with its European counterpart with new protocols that penalise an over-reliance on touchscreen menus. A manufacturer now loses points if it doesn’t provide either a physical button or stick or a permanently dedicated section of a touchscreen to engage indicators, hazard lights, windscreen wipers, headlights and sound the horn. However, a car penalised for distracting controls can recoup points in other areas to still achieve a 5-star overall rating. Ultimately, poor ANCAP ratings do not ban cars from the market. For Australia to follow in China’s path, the government would need to update the Australian Design Rules which govern the mandatory standards for all new vehicles in the market.

Advertisement

Dr Ingrid Johnston, chief executive of the ACRS, said there is now “a strong case for Australian authorities to review whether existing vehicle safety standards adequately address the distraction risks associated with modern touchscreen interfaces”. She said existing rules do not comprehensively assess the distraction or complexity associated with operating in-vehicle systems. Johnston said that when updating the requirements, authorities should consider the number of interactions required to complete common tasks, the time drivers spend looking away from the road, and whether complex functions should be restricted while driving. Related Article Road safety Chinese ban on Tesla-style door handles likely to flow through to Australia “ACRS would support consideration of stronger, evidence-based requirements, including whether frequently used or safety-critical functions should have physical controls or other interfaces that remain readily accessible without requiring prolonged visual attention,” Johnston said. Allianz, in calling for stricter car design rules, pointed to the findings of research it commissioned comprising a review of 80 studies on driver distraction, as well as new experiments using retina-tracking technology in real vehicles and analysis of claims data and more than 34,000 injury-causing crashes since 1999.

Advertisement

The review reassessed historical crashes for additional indicators of distraction such as a lack of braking or evasive action. While distraction is recorded as the cause in just 1.4 per cent of crashes, Allianz now believes distraction contributes to as many as one in three road crashes. Allianz also released survey data of Australian motorists which found 75 per cent of the 1200 respondents believe in-vehicle technology distractions have increased in recent years, with 41 per cent rating the risk of driver distraction as high or very high. About 29 per cent of respondents said they experienced a critical situation, such as hard braking, a near miss or a crash, while using a vehicle touchscreen. One in five Australian drivers surveyed reported causing or partly causing a crash in the past three years, with 67 per cent of those saying distraction definitely or possibly played a role. “Allianz’s studies also assessed how a distracted driver’s performance compared with an intoxicated driver, and found in certain scenarios such as on rural roads, a two-second glance away from the road can be more dangerous than a 0.08 blood alcohol content in a driver,” the review said. Michael Regan, an emeritus professor at the University of NSW who has studied road user behaviour and in-vehicle distraction, was critical of newer generation cars that required a touchscreen to adjust settings such as side mirrors, air conditioning and radio.

Advertisement

“It’s madness because it’s extremely distracting,” Michael Regan, emeritus professor at UNSW “It’s madness because it’s extremely distracting,” said Regan, who oversaw Allianz’s findings. “We know from research that when a driver takes their eyes off the road, they typically miss traffic signs, signals and subtle changes, and that means they take longer to react in the presence of danger, largely because they haven’t been able to predict it.” Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Uber forced to reinstate driver accused of speeding, sexual comments Regan cited studies which have found that when a driver looks away from the road for more than two seconds, their risk of having a crash doubles, and for every second after that the “risk rises exponentially”. “You’re not only taking you’re eyes off the road, you’re taking your mind off the road,” Regan said.

Advertisement

Whether car manufacturers agree to stricter design rules is unclear. Tony Weber, chief executive of the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries, which represents the industry, said Australia acting ahead of other jurisdictions could harm local supply and cost. “International harmonisation ensures Australians benefit from globally developed vehicle safety standards. Introducing additional Australian requirements could increase complexity and cost for consumers,” Weber said. A spokeswoman for Transport Minister Catherine King also noted the importance of international harmonisation for Australian Design Rules due to the nation’s reliance on vehicle imports. “The Australian government is continually adding to or amending Australian Design Rules (ADRs) based on changing vehicle technology and road safety risks,” she said. Amplia Therapeutics has delivered a sweeping update on its four-front clinical assault with lead drug narmafotinib, targeting some of the toughest cancers, including pancreatic, ovarian and lung cancer. Headlining the progress snapshot is an intriguing new clue from its key pancreatic cancer trial, suggesting the drug’s effectiveness may not depend on whether a patient’s tumour carries certain cancer-driving mutations in the KRAS gene. KRAS gene mutations are genetic changes that can cause cells to grow and divide uncontrollably, helping drive disease development. The gene normally acts like an on-off switch, controlling signals that tell cells when to grow. When mutated, the switch can become permanently stuck in the “on” position, encouraging cancer cells to multiply. Amplia Therapeutics is pushing ahead with four clinical trials for its lead drug narmafotinib in pancreatic, ovarian, and lung cancer (pancreatic cancer cells pictured). The finding is significant as pancreatic cancer treatment is rapidly shifting towards targeted therapies. KRAS gene mutations are found in more than 90 per cent of pancreatic cancers, making them a major focus for drug developers. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently approved a new KRAS-targeting drug that showed a significant survival benefit, highlighting the potential of this new class of therapies. Amplia’s data, however, suggest its Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) inhibitor narmafotinib could work alongside the KRAS drugs, potentially making it effective in a broader patient population or in powerful combination treatments.

Advertisement

‘It is exciting to be moving forward with these trials as the company build on positive clinical data.’ Amplia Therapeutics chief medical officer Dr Jason Lickliter Narmafotinib works by blocking a protein known as FAK, which is found at unusually high levels in solid tumours such as pancreatic cancer. The protein plays a key role in helping cancer cells grow, survive and resist treatment. FAK also contributes to the creation of dense, scar-like fibrotic tissue that forms a protective fortress around some tumours. By blocking FAK, the company believes narmafotinib can weaken or even break down this biological barrier, giving chemotherapy a cleaner shot at destroying the cancer cells within. Amplia’s ACCENT trial, which is evaluating narmafotinib combined with standard chemotherapy in newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic cancer patients, has delivered promising results. Previously reported data showed a significant response rate of 36 per cent, a median overall survival of 11.1 months and a complete response rate of a stunning 7.8 per cent, a figure considered historically rare in pancreatic cancer. The latest findings suggest the treatment may also have serious staying power, with two patients now having clocked a remarkable two years in the study and a third still receiving treatment after 19 months. Amplia Therapeutics chief medical officer Dr Jason Lickliter said: “It is exciting to be moving forward with these trials as the company builds on the positive clinical data from the ACCENT trial and the promising preclinical data underpinning the PRROSE and Lilly combination studies.”

Advertisement

While its ACCENT trial continues to deliver, the company has also advanced three other clinical trials into the late-stage start-up phase. The first, dubbed ACCENT-Mini, is being designed to evaluate a daily dosing regimen of narmafotinib in addition to chemotherapy at three Australian sites. Ethics approval is expected imminently, with safety and pharmacokinetic data anticipated in the first half of 2027. Management says this data will be crucial for its submission to the US FDA for a larger registrational study. The company is also tackling ovarian cancer with its PRROSE study, opening a second major front for its lead drug. The Australia New Zealand Gynaecological Oncology Group will run the trial in collaboration, sponsoring and coordinating it through its extensive network of more than 1650 members. Like ACCENT-Mini, the PRROSE trial will pair narmafotinib with established chemotherapy drugs, this time carboplatin and paclitaxel, targeting women with high-grade serous ovarian cancer who have shown a limited response to their initial treatment. The main goals are to assess the combination’s safety and explore whether it can increase the proportion of patients eligible for successful surgical resection. With the trial protocol finalised and ethics approval submitted, Amplia is nearing recruitment of 26 patients across Australia and New Zealand.

Advertisement

Rounding out the pipeline, the company is preparing a separate update on its trial combining narmafotinib with global pharmaceutical giant Lilly’s experimental KRAS G12C inhibitor, olomorasib. The study will target patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer, exploring the potential of attacking the disease on multiple fronts by combining drugs that target different cancer-driving pathways. Amplia believes blocking the FAK protein could help shut down a pathway cancer cells use to resist KRAS-targeted treatments. With four trials pushing ahead across a range of hard-to-treat cancers, Amplia appears to be methodically building a case for its cancer drug narmafotinib. The suggestion that its lead drug could work independently of the KRAS mutations that dominate pancreatic cancer might just be the key to unlocking its potential as a standalone or combination therapy in a field crying out for new options. Senior public servants repeatedly queried why NSW One Nation leader Mike Newman was charging taxpayers for hotels, trips and restaurant bills, including a $7791 dinner with a Japanese trade delegation which included 71 beers and 23 bottles of wine. Documents released through parliament on Thursday show senior bureaucrats rebuked Newman for his spending habits during his 28-month stint as a senior trade commissioner in Japan, with one executive rejecting a $211 bill for lunch and telling the now-One Nation leader it was “not how the NSW government does business”. It comes after this masthead last week revealed Newman racked up hundreds of thousands of dollars in expenses for taxpayer-funded flights, five-star hotels and restaurant and bar bills during his 28-month stint as a senior trade commissioner in Japan. The spending included about $20,494 on a seven-month stay in a Meriton Suite in Sydney before he moved to Japan. The spending occurred while he waited for permission to travel to Japan during the COVID-19 pandemic, despite Newman living in Sydney when he was appointed.

Advertisement

He was also charging taxpayers about $8000 a month to rent an apartment in Tokyo for some of that time. The spending was revealed in the context of Newman’s repeated criticisms of the NSW public service since his appointment as One Nation’s leader in NSW, in which he raised the prospect of “claw[ing] back entitlements from those found responsible for having egregiously misused public funds without consequences”. Mike Newman is the candidate for Cessnock and the One Nation leader in NSW. James Brickwood “There is so much money and waste that is inside the public service,” he said during his unveiling in August. But the documents released on Thursday shed new light on some of the expenses, as well as revealing the public service repeatedly questioned Newman’s spending. This masthead previously reported Newman charged taxpayers for a bill adding up to almost $5300 at Crystalbrook Kingsley, a hotel in Newcastle, in August 2023. He said that had been for a dinner with a Japanese trade delegation and spending on alcohol was pre-approved.

Advertisement

But the documents show the bill was larger – $7790.50 – and reveal public servants said they were only told that alcohol would be served at the event. The bill, for 51 people, included a three-course meal at $109 per head, as well as 71 beers and 23 bottles of wine. The restaurant charged $59 per bottle. The documents show that spending was later closely scrutinised, with an official forced to answer a series of questions about how it had occurred. The official – whose name was redacted – noted that only one onshore Investment NSW staffer was at the event, and that Newman had “hosted the dinner”. The dinner was aimed at “facilitating connections” with the Japanese delegation, NSW officials and “academia” and “fostering ongoing dialogue”, they wrote, and resulted in “further discussions” on potential “partnerships and investment opportunities”. The official said they had found out Newman and the Department of Regional NSW had been planning “some kind of dinner” about a month earlier. However, they said, it was “only at the event itself that we found out that alcohol was being served and that Mike Newman was intending to pay for all of it”.

NSW Votes The long list of former Coalition MPs seeking new home on One Nation’s crowded NSW ticket Newman previously defended his spending and pointed to cases of using his own money to fund trips, such as in October 2023, when he said he spent about $10,000 to attend an Australia-Japan Business Council event in Melbourne because the government would not approve it. Some documents also show Newman paid his own per diem during some business trips. The One Nation leader said he had saved taxpayers by arguing against a $49 million net zero economy office the government wanted to establish, though this masthead has been unable to verify that claim. “I should be bloody given congratulations, not censured, for stopping a $50 million empire going in that was going to be a complete waste of money,” he said. Not all the documents obtained through a parliamentary call for papers have been publicly released, and Newman said there was important “contextual” information in emails he had sent to the department.

“Senior management and I did not see eye to eye because we had very strong differences of opinion on doing business,” he said. “My department wanted to issue a fatwa on me [and] they used to use technicalities and irrelevant stuff to go after me because I threatened the status quo. “I’m not a hypocrite, I was paying for a lot of this stuff myself.” Among the other expenses was another month-long stay at the Meriton Suites in North Sydney in 2023 for which he billed taxpayers $5086. Documents show public servants questioned that spending, and wrote to Newman asking why he was staying in the hotel for 32 nights, longer than had been approved. The public servant notes the department had approved 25 days despite already having “concerns [it] was an extensive period out of market”. “What’s the reason for the extra first week before the approved travel date?” they wrote.

One Nation Revealed: One Nation leader’s seven-month Sydney hotel stay that cost taxpayers $20,000 Newman – who also took personal leave during that period – said he had booked a longer trip to get a discount, and had paid for his own personal leave as well as his accommodation while in Newcastle for the Crystalbrook Kingsley event. It is unclear if all of the spending revealed through the documents was approved. However, in another, a public servant noted they would reject a $211 bill Newman had sought to charge taxpayers for a business lunch at Glorietta in North Sydney. “At $70 per head (including wine), this exceeds a reasonable cost for lunch, noting that such hospitality and entertainment is not how the NSW government does business with the private sector,” the official wrote. Newman said the meal had been with a senior executive, and that the client had ordered a $17 glass of wine and another Investment NSW staff member had ordered an expensive prawn salad. “I could hardly take a person like that to the food hall at North Sydney station,” he said. Many years ago, we had a ping-pong table in our office. At the time we thought it was the coolest perk in the world – a way for employees to play and let off steam most afternoons. It now feels like a quaint inclusion, especially when modern workplaces spend big dollars on ways to engage their staff, from overseas meet-ups to long lunches, on-site wellness centres to ergonomic workstations. Once the ultimate indicator of office perks, the table tennis table now is less common in modern workspaces. Bloomberg However, none of that matters if you don’t have a healthy work environment in the first place. Instead of throwing money at the problem, here are 10 small, repeatable behaviours that anyone can do to improve their workplace right now, without waiting for the ping pong table to arrive. 1. Swap meetings for walks. The next time you have a one-on-one meeting with a colleague that doesn’t require a screen, suggest that you take it outside. Walk around the block, or to the closest park, and you’ll have better conversations and get more exercise than spending yet another meeting staring at the blank office wall.

Advertisement

2. Give credit where it’s due. The simplest way of showing appreciation is by acknowledging it in public. When someone does something that’s worth praising, say it out loud, on the spot, ideally to their face. Extra points if you also voice it in an all-staff meeting, or on a group email, so everyone can see. 3. Ask more questions than you answer. The smartest person in the room is the most curious. When you ask questions with an open mind, you’re ensuring you properly understand what’s going on. You never want to be the person who just talks over everyone, so listen more than you speak. Any one of these can save you money, time, pain and heartache if you incorporate them into your everyday working life. 4. Treat mistakes as learning opportunities. Everyone stuffs up, but it’s what you do next that sets the cultural tone. When you weaponise mistakes so that people are too scared to fail, you’re creating a toxic work environment. Think of every error as a way of improving the process so that it’s even better the next time. 5. Set expectations and meet them. The simplest definition of trust is what happens when you set clear expectations and meet them. In the workplace, tell your colleagues what you’re going to do, and then do it. That builds trust over the long term, one of the key components of a healthy working environment.

Advertisement

6. When in doubt, over-communicate. Work is a team sport, and you should include as many people as possible in the successes that you can. One way to do that is to over-communicate – not by CCing the world on every email, but by bringing people along so they understand the why behind your actions. Editor's pick Opinion

Holidays Why it’s time for you to ditch taking long annual holidays Tim Duggan Work columnist 7. Treat leave as leave. When someone’s out of the office, let them be out of the office. It doesn’t matter whether it’s sickness, bereavement, maternity or annual leave, give people the mental space to not think about work when they’re not there. 8. End every meeting with an action. We’ve all been in meetings that last forever and then end with nothing much to show for it. Close out every single meeting with at least one action item, then write it down to ensure it’s followed up on. 9. Make generous assumptions. Of course, you can be wary of other people’s motivations, but what might happen if you made “generous assumptions” instead? These are the beliefs that someone is acting with good intentions instead of automatically assuming they are not. It can really change how you think about everyone around you.

Advertisement

10. Give good handovers. The difference between success and failure in a project is often the quality of the handover. This means fully explaining the progress of where things are at – both good and bad – every time you move roles, go on leave, or finish up at a job. Any one of these can save you money, time, pain and heartache if you incorporate them into your everyday working life. Recognition, feedback and productive workplaces are linked with higher engagement, retention, and healthier teams. These simple habits don’t cost a cent, but they are really worth their weight in gold. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
